# Dimension 5 — Running Codex inside OpenShell / `openshell-sandbox`

The concrete delta to run a Codex session where a Claude Code session runs
today. Source details in [citations](../citations.md).

**Two kinds of evidence appear in this file and they are labelled throughout.**

- **[N]** — a web source fetched in-session, as in every other reference file.
- **(local)** — a fact read directly from the user's own repos at
  `/sandbox/source/openshell-sandbox/` and `/sandbox/source/openshell-policy.yaml`.
  These are verifiable on the machine but are not citations, and they cannot
  substitute for a cited claim about Codex's behaviour.

## The current shape (local)

- The image installs the agent with
  `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code @googleworkspace/cli`
  (`Containerfile:23`) on Node 22 from NodeSource (`Containerfile:18-19`).
  `dtach` is installed for TUI persistence (`Containerfile:14`); screen and tmux
  were tested and rejected because they mangle the TUI.
- The effective policy sets `landlock: compatibility: best_effort` and
  `process: run_as_user: sandbox` / `run_as_group: sandbox`
  (`openshell-policy.yaml`). **The container already runs as a non-root user and
  OpenShell already applies Landlock.**
- The `anthropic_api` policy block allows exactly five hosts on port 443:
  `api.anthropic.com`, `console.anthropic.com`, `platform.claude.com`,
  `claude.ai`, `statsig.anthropic.com`. Every endpoint carries both
  `protocol: rest` and `enforcement: enforce`.
- Egress is forced through OpenShell's HTTP CONNECT proxy at `10.200.0.1:3128`;
  OpenShell injects `ALL_PROXY` plus lowercase `http_proxy`/`https_proxy`/
  `no_proxy` into sandbox processes, and `ALL_PROXY` overrides a user-set
  `HTTPS_PROXY` (repo `CLAUDE.md`, OpenShell Policy Gotchas 18 and 19).
- OAuth is preserved across `--recreate` by uploading `.claude.json` and
  `.credentials.json`.
- The agent runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` by design: "Network
  policy (L4/L7), Landlock filesystem, and process isolation replace Claude's
  permission system" (repo `CLAUDE.md`, rule 1).

Everything below is what changes.

## 1. Codex's own sandbox must be turned off — and OpenAI says so

Codex's Linux sandbox is **not** what the earlier GitHub issues describe.

> "Linux uses `bwrap` plus `seccomp` by default." [20]

> "Windows uses the Linux sandbox implementation when running in Windows
> Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL2). WSL1 was supported through Codex 0.114; starting
> in **0.115**, the Linux sandbox moved to `bwrap`, so WSL1 is no longer
> supported." [20]

Landlock survives only as a fallback:

> "On Linux and WSL, Codex uses bubblewrap and seccomp, with Landlock available
> for compatibility fallback paths. The strongest enforcement path depends on
> user namespaces and kernel support; **restricted container hosts can force
> compatibility paths, and unsupported split policies are refused.**" [14]

The bubblewrap prerequisite is a hard install dependency, and the fallback has
its own requirement:

> "On Linux and WSL2, install bubblewrap with your package manager first…
> Codex uses the first `bwrap` executable it finds on `PATH`. If no `bwrap`
> executable is available, Codex falls back to a bundled helper, but that helper
> **requires support for unprivileged user namespace creation**." [19]

> "Codex surfaces a startup warning when `bwrap` is missing or when the helper
> can't create the needed user namespace." [19]

OpenAI's guidance for exactly this situation is unambiguous:

> "When you run Linux in a containerized environment such as Docker, the sandbox
> may not work if the host or container configuration blocks the namespace,
> setuid `bwrap`, or seccomp operations that Codex needs. In that case,
> configure your Docker container to provide the isolation you need, then run
> codex with `--sandbox danger-full-access` (or the
> `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` flag) inside the container." [20]

> "**If the container is your intended security boundary, run Codex with
> `--sandbox danger-full-access` inside the container so Codex does not try to
> create a second sandbox layer.**" [20]

That is the wrapper's rule 1, in OpenAI's words. And OpenAI's own reference
"secure" devcontainer does exactly this — `containerEnv` sets
**`CODEX_UNSAFE_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX=1`** alongside `CODEX_ENABLE_FIREWALL=1` [47].
(No fetched page documents that variable's semantics; the name and its use in
that file are the whole of the evidence.)

**Delta:** `--dangerously-skip-permissions` becomes
`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` (alias `--yolo`), or the pair
`--sandbox danger-full-access --ask-for-approval never` [20]. `--full-auto` is
**not** the equivalent — it is deprecated and "Codex prints a warning when this
flag is used" [9].

**Two risks to plan for.**

*Risk A — this may be blocked by policy.* An enterprise `requirements.toml` can
constrain `allowed_sandbox_modes` and `allowed_approval_policies` [1]. If the
ChatGPT workspace is managed, `danger-full-access` may simply not be selectable.
Verify before committing.

*Risk B — the failure mode if the sandbox is left on is not benign.* The
historical Landlock-era reports are the wrong evidence (see below), but the
current docs only promise that the sandbox "may not work". Two dated reports of
what "may not work" looked like:

- Issue #9292, opened 2026-01-15, **Closed**: `error running landlock: Io(Os {
  code: 1, kind: PermissionDenied, message: "Operation not permitted" })` on
  Ubuntu 24.04.3, kernel 6.14.0-37, with
  `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1` and
  `/sys/kernel/security/landlock` missing. Version matrix: 0.79.0 works, 0.80.0
  works, 0.81.0 fails, 0.84.0 fails. The reporter's conclusion: "Only
  `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` works." [43]
- A forum report of `Filesystem sandbox: read-only` from
  `codex --sandbox=danger-full-access --ask-for-approval=never exec …` inside a
  Docker volume, with a reply suggesting flag placement after the `exec`
  subcommand mattered [64]. Unverified user content, no OpenAI confirmation.
- Issue #2267, opened 2025-08-13, still **Open**: `error running landlock:
  Sandbox(LandlockRestrict)` on codex-cli 0.21.0, NixOS [42].

**All three predate the 0.115 move to bwrap.** They establish that the pattern
of container-nesting failure is real and recurring; they do **not** establish
how the current bwrap implementation behaves under rootless Podman. Nothing
found in this research tests that.

**The specific unknown:** the wrapper's Podman container runs as the unprivileged
user `sandbox` (local), and the bundled `bwrap` fallback "requires support for
unprivileged user namespace creation" [19]. Whether a rootless-Podman container
grants that is not answered by any source in this pool. **The lazy and correct
move is to not find out — disable the inner sandbox, which is what OpenAI
prescribes anyway.**

For contrast, note what OpenAI's own tooling assumes when it *does* keep the
sandbox on: `run_in_container.sh` requires `--cap-add=NET_ADMIN
--cap-add=NET_RAW`, makes four `docker exec --user root` calls, and hard-codes
`docker` throughout [45]; `devcontainer.secure.json` adds seven capabilities
(`SYS_ADMIN`, `SYS_CHROOT`, `SETUID`, `SETGID`, `SYS_PTRACE`, `NET_ADMIN`,
`NET_RAW`) plus `seccomp=unconfined` and `apparmor=unconfined` [47]. **Neither
is compatible with a rootless-Podman sandbox whose whole point is that the
container has no such privileges.** (It does *not* set `privileged`, and it does
run as `remoteUser: vscode` rather than root [47].)

## 2. The proxy question — the highest-risk open item

This is the one that decides whether Codex works at all in this environment, and
the documentation does not answer it.

**What is established.** The published environment-variable list [15] contains
twelve variables — `CODEX_HOME`, `CODEX_SQLITE_HOME`, `CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE`,
`CODEX_INSTALL_DIR`, `CODEX_API_KEY`, `CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN`,
`OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID`, `OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE`,
`OPENAI_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_CONTEXT`, `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE`, `SSL_CERT_FILE`,
`RUST_LOG` — and **no proxy variable of any kind**. The page's own scope note
limits how far that goes: "This page lists stable public environment variables
that Codex reads directly. It does not list internal development variables, test
variables, or provider-specific secret names…" [15]

The permissions page confirms a separate mechanism exists but names nothing:

> "**Codex service traffic**: Model, authentication, and other client service
> requests use the client's separate HTTP and system-proxy settings." [14]

**The history.** PR #3455, "Use of HTTP_PROXY env var in reqwest clients", would
have added `apply_env_proxy` honouring `HTTPS_PROXY → HTTP_PROXY → ALL_PROXY`
across the login and Ollama clients. Opened 2025-09-11, **closed unmerged on
2025-10-30** with:

> "we're currently accepting contributions for bugs and security fixes, but
> we're not generally accepting new features at this time" [44]

— process grounds, not technical rejection. Its successor issue #4242, "Use
proxy environment variables across Codex HTTP clients", was **still Open** as
fetched [41], and its framing is the diagnosis: "Today users behind corporate
proxies must patch individual call sites (login, Ollama, etc.)". `NO_PROXY` was
explicitly out of scope even in the PR [44].

**Verdict: there is no documented guarantee that the Codex CLI routes its own
model and auth traffic through `HTTPS_PROXY`.** It may do so anyway via
`reqwest`'s or the OS's defaults — that is exactly what [14] hints at without
naming — but this research could not confirm it.

**A second, separate hazard specific to this environment.** Codex has its own
sandboxed-command network proxy, and if enabled it **overwrites** the proxy
variables inside the sandbox:

> `permissions.<name>.network.proxy_url` — "HTTP proxy listener used for
> `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, websocket proxy variables, and related tool proxy
> environment variables." Default `http://127.0.0.1:3128`. [14]

Note the collision: Codex's default listener port is **3128**, the same port
OpenShell's CONNECT proxy uses at `10.200.0.1:3128` (local). Two mitigations
exist in the same table: `features.network_proxy.enabled` defaults to `false`
[1], and `allow_upstream_proxy` defaults to `true` — "Lets sandboxed networking
honor an upstream proxy from the environment" [14]. **Leave
`features.network_proxy` off.** The outer policy is already the boundary, and
turning it on adds a second proxy layer that competes for the same env vars and
the same port number.

Codex's proxy also does not cover what a security reviewer might assume it does:

> "The network proxy filters scripts, programs, and child processes that run
> inside the local command sandbox. It does not filter web search, app or
> connector tool calls, MCP server connections, browser or Computer Use
> activity, Codex cloud tasks, or the client's model and authentication
> requests." [14]

> "A command network allowlist is not a global network policy for every action
> Codex can perform." [14]

For this setup that is reassuring rather than alarming: the OpenShell policy *is*
a global network policy, applied below Codex, and it catches everything Codex's
own allowlist would miss.

**TLS interception is documented and does work by env var** [4][15]:

> "If your network uses a corporate TLS proxy or private root CA, set
> `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE` to a PEM bundle before logging in. When
> `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE` is unset, Codex falls back to `SSL_CERT_FILE`. The same
> custom CA settings apply to login, normal HTTPS requests, and secure WebSocket
> connections." [4]

## 3. Network policy — which hosts to allow

**This research could not establish the Codex CLI's runtime egress set.** No
fetched page enumerates the hostnames it contacts, and the page most likely to —
`learn.chatgpt.com/docs/internet-access` — returned **404** [69].

What *is* attributable to Codex itself:

| Host | Why | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `chatgpt.com` | installer (`/codex/install.sh`, `/codex/install.ps1`); MCP OAuth CIMD documents at `/oauth/codex/<callback_id>/client.json` | [37][13] |
| `releases.openai.com` | standalone installer download source, "by default" | [37] |
| `api.openai.com` | the mandatory reachability probe in OpenAI's own firewall script, and its single-domain fallback allowlist | [46] |
| `auth.openai.com` | appears in OpenAI's reference devcontainer allowlist, with no doc text attributing it to login | [47] |

OpenAI's reference devcontainer allows 14 domains [47]:

```
api.openai.com auth.openai.com github.com api.github.com codeload.github.com
raw.githubusercontent.com objects.githubusercontent.com crates.io index.crates.io
static.crates.io static.rust-lang.org registry.npmjs.org pypi.org files.pythonhosted.org
```

**Read that correctly.** That container exists to develop the Codex Rust
repository — `crates.io`, `static.rust-lang.org`, `registry.npmjs.org`, `pypi.org`
and `files.pythonhosted.org` are build traffic for *that* project, not Codex's
egress. It is a superset skewed by its purpose, not an answer.

The firewall script's fallback is the more informative datum: when
`/etc/codex/allowed_domains.txt` is missing, `init-firewall.sh` allows exactly
one domain, `api.openai.com`, and then **verifies** that `https://api.openai.com`
is reachable and `https://example.com` is not [46]. `run_in_container.sh`
likewise defaults `OPENAI_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` to `api.openai.com` [45]. That is a
strong hint that `api.openai.com` alone suffices for API-key operation, but it
is a hint from a reference script, not a statement.

(Caveat on that script: nothing in `init-firewall.sh` actually reads
`OPENAI_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` — it reads `/etc/codex/allowed_domains.txt`. Whatever
bridges the two was not fetched [46].)

**Practical delta.** The `anthropic_api` policy block (local) would become a
`codex_api` block. A defensible starting list, with confidence levels stated:

| Host | Port | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| `api.openai.com` | 443 | **High** — OpenAI's own firewall requires it reachable [46] |
| `chatgpt.com` | 443 | **High** for installer and MCP OAuth [37][13]; **inferred** for ChatGPT-plan model traffic |
| `auth.openai.com` | 443 | **Medium** — in OpenAI's allowlist [47], unattributed in docs |
| `releases.openai.com` | 443 | **High**, install/update only [37] |

Every OpenShell endpoint needs both `protocol: rest` and `enforcement: enforce`
(local, gotcha 22), and `**.openai.com` matches apex plus subdomains where
`*.openai.com` matches one level (local, gotcha 3).

**This list is a starting hypothesis, not a verified egress set.** The honest
method is to apply it, run a session, and read the 403s from the egress proxy —
OpenShell policies hot-update on running sandboxes
(`openshell policy set --policy <file> <name>`, local gotcha 14), so iterating
is cheap.

## 4. Authentication without a browser

Three documented paths, in descending order of fit for this environment [4]:

1. **API key, non-interactive** —
   `printenv OPENAI_API_KEY | codex login --with-api-key`. OpenAI's own
   recommendation: "Use API key authentication for programmatic Codex CLI
   workflows, such as CI/CD jobs" and "API keys are still the recommended
   default for automation" [4]. Cost consequence: "Codex uses standard API
   pricing instead of included ChatGPT plan credits", and **Codex cloud becomes
   unavailable** — "Codex cloud requires signing in with ChatGPT" [4].
2. **Copy the credential cache from the host** — the exact analogue of the
   wrapper's existing `.claude.json` + `.credentials.json` upload. OpenAI
   documents the container form [4]:
   ```
   CONTAINER_HOME=$(docker exec MY_CONTAINER printenv HOME)
   docker exec MY_CONTAINER mkdir -p "$CONTAINER_HOME/.codex"
   docker cp ~/.codex/auth.json MY_CONTAINER:"$CONTAINER_HOME/.codex/auth.json"
   ```
   The single file is **`~/.codex/auth.json`** — simpler than the two-file
   Claude Code case. Caveat from the same page: "If your OS stores credentials
   in a credential store instead of `~/.codex/auth.json`, this method may not
   apply" — so the host must be on `cli_auth_credentials_store = "file"` [4].
   For token refresh to survive, `chatgpt.com` (or whatever host serves refresh)
   must be reachable; "Codex refreshes tokens automatically during use before
   they expire" [4].
3. **Device code (beta)** — `codex login --device-auth`, but it is
   administratively gateable and fails with `"Please contact your workspace
   admin to enable device code authentication"` when disabled [4][40].

A fourth path exists but needs a port hole: tunnelling "Codex's local callback
server (default **`localhost:1455`**)" [4]. In a sandbox with no browser and a
loopback-restricted policy this is the least attractive option.

**Delta:** the wrapper's `.claude.json` + `.credentials.json` upload becomes a
single `~/.codex/auth.json` upload, or is replaced entirely by an
`OPENAI_API_KEY` in `/sandbox/.env` piped through
`codex login --with-api-key` at container start.

## 5. Everything else that changes

| Wrapper component (local) | Codex equivalent | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` | `npm install -g @openai/codex` [37] | One line in `Containerfile` |
| `config/sandbox-claude.md` → `/sandbox/source/CLAUDE.md` | `AGENTS.md` at the same path [5] | Rename; **but see the 32 KiB cap below** |
| `--dangerously-skip-permissions` | `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` [20] | Flag swap in `claude-wrapper.sh` |
| `--model claude-opus-5[1m]` for personal/home | `--model gpt-5.6-sol` or `model` in `config.toml` [7] | Straight swap |
| `.claude.json` + `.credentials.json` | `~/.codex/auth.json` [4] | Simpler |
| `~/.claude/` upload (skills, settings, plugins) | `~/.codex/` plus `~/.agents/skills/` [21] | Two upload targets instead of one |
| `strip-settings.py` (strips model-pinning env vars from `settings.json`) | Would need rewriting against `config.toml` | Rewrite |
| Dummy OTEL hooks (`python3 -c ""`) to force telemetry emission | Codex has a first-class `otel` config surface [1][3] | **Delete, do not port** |
| `dtach` TUI persistence | Unknown — no source tested Codex's TUI under `dtach` | Must be tested |
| `validate-profile.sh` net checks against Anthropic hosts | Repoint at OpenAI hosts | Mechanical |

**Two size traps.**

*AGENTS.md is capped and CLAUDE.md is not.* Codex "stops adding files once the
combined size reaches the limit defined by `project_doc_max_bytes` (32 KiB by
default)" [5]. Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md files "in full regardless of length",
guidance being "under 200 lines" [54]. The wrapper's base system prompt plus
per-profile fragment plus every repo's own instructions all concatenate into one
chain — **a set of files Claude Code accepts can be silently truncated by
Codex.** `project_doc_max_bytes = 65536` is the documented lever [5]. (Note the
unresolved ambiguity about whether the cap is per-file or combined, in
[setup-and-installation](setup-and-installation.md).)

*Project config is gated on trust and drops ten keys.* Codex loads
`.codex/config.toml` "only when you trust the project" [2], and silently ignores
`model_provider`, `model_providers`, `openai_base_url`, `notify`, `otel` and
five more at project scope, printing a startup warning [1][3]. Anything the
wrapper wants enforced must go in the **user-level** `~/.codex/config.toml`
uploaded at create time, and trust must be pre-seeded via
`projects.<path>.trust_level = "trusted"` [1] or every project layer is inert.

*Hooks are inert until trusted.* "Codex records trust against the hook's current
hash, so new or changed hooks are marked for review and skipped until trusted"
[10]. In a non-interactive sandbox that means either
`--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` [9] or managed hooks via `requirements.toml`
with `allow_managed_hooks_only = true` [48] — whose on-disk location this
research could not establish.

## 6. What Codex cloud is, for contrast

Not the same thing as this sandbox, and worth not conflating:

> "Codex cloud: Runs in isolated OpenAI-managed containers… Uses a two-phase
> runtime model: setup runs before the agent phase and can access the network to
> install specified dependencies, then **the agent phase runs offline by
> default** unless you enable internet access for that environment. Secrets
> configured for cloud environments are available only during setup and are
> removed before the agent phase starts." [20]

That is a materially stricter default than the wrapper's (which allows npm,
PyPI and Debian throughout). It also requires ChatGPT sign-in and is unavailable
on an API key [4]. `codex-universal` is the published reference image for that
environment — "This is not an identical environment but should help for
debugging and development" — and notably says nothing about bubblewrap, seccomp,
the Codex sandbox, its base image, or root [38].

## Gaps and limitations

1. **Nothing in the fetched set names rootless Podman.** Container guidance is
   Docker and Dev Containers only [20][45][47]. Every rootless-specific claim
   here is inference and is marked as such.
2. **The Codex CLI's runtime egress set is not published.** [69] returned 404.
   The host list in §3 is a hypothesis to test, not a verified list.
3. **Whether Codex honours `HTTPS_PROXY` for its own model/auth traffic is
   unresolved** [14][15][41][44]. This is the single highest-risk unknown; if it
   does not, Codex cannot reach the model through a CONNECT-only egress at all.
4. **Update-check behaviour offline is entirely undocumented.** The key
   `check_for_update_on_startup` appears in the `requirements.toml` table with
   the note "set to `false` only when updates are centrally managed" [1], and no
   fetched page describes what happens when the check cannot reach the network.
5. **Whether the bwrap-era (0.115+) sandbox fails under rootless Podman, and
   with what error, is untested by any source.** All three failure reports
   [42][43][64] are Landlock-era.
6. `CODEX_UNSAFE_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX` appears only in a config file [47]; its
   semantics are undocumented.
7. `developers.openai.com/codex/security` turned out to document a different
   product (application-security scanning) and contributed nothing [18] — and
   it is precisely where the repository's `docs/sandbox.md` redirects, that file
   being a three-line stub with zero technical content [49]. Reading the repo
   for sandbox documentation is a dead end in both directions.
8. `dtach` compatibility with the Codex TUI is untested and unsourced.
9. `requirements.toml`'s on-disk path is unknown, which blocks the managed-hooks
   route in §5.
